results.title: Which Evaluation metrics serves better, RMSE or MAE? - Kaggle
results.content: Gaurav Rajesh Sahani · Posted 3 years ago in Questions & Answers # Which Evaluation metrics serves better, RMSE or MAE? RMSE penalizes large errors more than MAE due to the fact that errors are squared initially. Both Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) and Mean Absolute Error (MAE) are commonly used metrics for evaluating the performance of regression models. However, they differ in how they measure the error between predicted and actual values, and which one serves better depends on the specific problem. RMSE measures the square root of the average of the squared differences between predicted and actual values. For example, in the case of predicting housing prices, large errors in prediction may have a significant impact on the value of the property, and therefore, RMSE would be a suitable evaluation metric. MAE measures the average of the absolute differences between predicted and actual values. For example, in the case of predicting the age of a person, small errors in prediction may be as significant as large errors, and therefore, MAE would be a suitable evaluation metric. The predicted ages and actual ages are as follows: The RMSE and MAE for this model are calculated as follows: RMSE = sqrt(1/10 \* sum((predicted\_age - actual\_age)^2)) = sqrt(31) = 5.57 MAE = 1/10 \* sum(abs(predicted\_age - actual\_age)) = 2.5 In this example, the MAE is smaller than the RMSE, indicating that MAE would be a better evaluation metric for this problem. In conclusion, both RMSE and MAE are useful evaluation metrics for regression models, but the choice of metric depends on the specific problem and the goals of the analysis. RMSE is suitable when large errors are more significant than small errors and when errors have a Gaussian distribution, while MAE is suitable when small errors are as significant as large errors and when errors have a non-Gaussian distribution. If you would like to give more weights to observations that are further from the mean (i.e. if being “off” by 20 is more than twice as bad as being off by 10″) then it’s better to use the RMSE to measure error because the RMSE is more sensitive to observations that are further from the mean.
